opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the important dynamics is that inference-time compute creates a gap between when a capability first *exists* and when it's cheap enough to use widely.

With pretraining-style scaling, once you've trained the model, the capability is mostly baked in, and the per-query cost is roughly fixed. With inference-time scaling, you can often get a capability early by spending a huge amount of compute per task: running the model for a very long time, sampling many attempts, doing lots of verification. So the first demonstration of something like "the AI can do a week-long software engineering project" might happen at a cost that's comparable to, or even more than, just paying a human. At that point it's technically possible but not economically transformative.

Then you get this fairly rapid cost decline afterward. Historically, the cost to reach a given level of performance has dropped by something like an order of magnitude or more per year, from algorithmic improvements, distillation, better hardware, and labs just optimizing serving. So my rough mental model is that there's a lag of maybe a year or so between "first achievable at very high cost" and "practical to deploy at scale," and that lag is somewhat predictable.

I think that has a few implications. One is that it gives you some warning. If you see a lab demonstrate a capability with massive inference spend, you should expect it to be broadly available fairly soon after, so the expensive demos are a leading indicator. That's useful for safety, for policy, and for people trying to forecast.

Another implication is that it matters a lot for the most important use cases, which I think are AI R&D in particular. AI companies are willing to pay much more per task than a typical customer, because the value of accelerating your own research is enormous. So for internal use, a capability might become "practical" much earlier than it does for the broad economy. You could have a situation where AIs are substantially speeding up AI research internally while the external world sees relatively little, because external deployment isn't cost-effective yet or the company just chooses not to deploy. That makes things less visible, which I think is somewhat concerning.

And then the third point is that inference compute is a fungible resource. If you have a lot of chips, you can trade them off between running many copies of a model and running fewer copies with more thinking each. So once you have AIs that are roughly at the level of good human researchers, the question of how many effective researchers you have becomes a question about how much compute you have and how efficiently you're spending it. That could lead to pretty fast scale-up after the capability threshold is crossed, which is part of why I take the possibility of fast takeoff dynamics seriously.

I'd add some uncertainty, though. Inference scaling doesn't help equally for all tasks. It's most effective where you can verify outputs or where there's a clear signal to iterate on, things like math, coding, things with tests. For fuzzier, longer-horizon tasks, just throwing more inference at it may hit diminishing returns faster, so the gap I described might look different there.

r001.rationale: The response says inference can involve running the model for a long time, but does not identify serial reasoning as a reason it may answer more slowly than a human.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes a capability that first exists at very high inference cost from one that is cheap enough to deploy widely.

r003.rationale: It says pretraining capabilities are mostly baked in and per-query cost is roughly fixed, but does not say they could be deployed immediately in vast numbers of model instances.

r004.rationale: It lists distillation as one source of cost decline, but does not clearly state that high-inference capabilities can be distilled quickly into models needing less inference compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different things going on here, and it's worth separating them out.

The first thing is just that inference-time compute lets you get capabilities earlier than you would otherwise get them, but at a cost. So if you have some task where the model can do it if you let it think for a long time, or sample a bunch of times and pick the best, or run some kind of search over its outputs, then in some sense the capability exists before it's cheap. And then the question of when it becomes practical to deploy at scale is really a question about when the cost comes down enough that it's worth it for the thing you want to use it for.

And I think the key dynamic is that these two things trade off. If you can get a capability by spending, say, a thousand times more inference compute, then you can typically also get that same capability by training a somewhat bigger model, or by doing more RL, or by distilling the expensive thinking into a cheaper model. So inference compute kind of functions as a preview. It tells you what the next generation is going to be able to do cheaply. Historically, people have talked about there being something like a rough exchange rate, where a 10x in inference compute buys you something like what you'd get from a pretty meaningful increase in training compute, though I'd be cautious about treating that as a fixed constant, because it varies a lot by task.

The second thing is that the economics of deployment are really different for different kinds of tasks. For a lot of consumer uses, where you're answering a chat query and the value of each query is small, spending a hundred dollars of compute on it is obviously not going to happen. But for things like AI R&D, or automating software engineering at a company that's paying engineers a lot of money, or doing security research, the value per task can be high enough that you're willing to spend quite a lot. So I expect inference-time compute to make capabilities practical first in the domains where the value of a task is high and where you can verify the output reasonably well, because verification is what makes things like best-of-n or search actually work. And then it diffuses out to lower-value uses as the cost comes down.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most important one from my perspective, is what this does to AI labs internally. Because labs are the ones who have the most willingness to spend compute on running their own models, and they're the ones with the highest-value tasks, which is speeding up their own research. So I think the first place you'll see really heavy inference-time scaling deployed at scale is not in products, it's in labs using lots of compute to run agents that do ML research. And that's where I think the acceleration dynamics get kind of concerning, because the point at which something becomes practical for a lab internally can be substantially earlier than when it shows up externally, and that gap could matter a lot for how much warning the rest of the world gets.

One more thing I'd flag is that it changes how you should think about forecasting. If you're trying to predict when some capability arrives, you kind of have to ask "at what cost?" It's not a single date anymore. There's a date at which it's achievable with a huge amount of compute, and a later date at which it's cheap, and depending on what you care about, you might care about either one. For something like dangerous capabilities, you probably care more about the first one, because a well-resourced actor can pay the cost. For broad economic transformation, you care more about the second.

So, to actually answer the question: I think it makes capabilities practical to deploy somewhat earlier than you'd naively expect, especially in high-value domains, and it makes the overall trajectory smoother in some sense, because you get this continuous dial you can turn rather than waiting for a discrete new model. But I don't think it fundamentally changes the picture that much relative to just continued scaling of training. It's more that it gives you an earlier and noisier preview of what's coming.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between when you can first get an AI to do something and when it’s cheap enough to use for that thing at a large scale. Inference-time compute can move the first of those forward quite a bit without immediately moving the second forward by the same amount.

Suppose you can get a model to solve a difficult problem by having it spend a huge amount of time reasoning, or by trying lots of different approaches and checking which ones work. That could be worthwhile for a particularly valuable problem. But it doesn’t necessarily mean you can afford to run that process millions of times a day.

Then, as models and inference become more efficient, that same capability might become much cheaper. So you could have a period where we know a capability is possible, and it’s being used in some expensive, specialized applications, before it becomes widespread.

The important caveat is that some applications are valuable enough that even very expensive inference is worth paying for. AI research could be an example: if spending a lot of compute lets you make a useful research advance, that could justify the cost. So I wouldn’t assume that a capability has to be cheap enough for mass deployment before it starts having significant effects.

r002.rationale: It clearly says inference-time compute can make a capability possible before it is cheap enough for large-scale use.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss pure pretraining scaling or immediate deployment across vast numbers of model instances.

r004.rationale: It says improved model and inference efficiency can lower costs, but does not express an expectation that capabilities will be distilled relatively quickly into models needing less inference compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes the distinction between being able to do something at all and being able to do it cheaply much more important. You might first demonstrate a capability by spending an enormous amount of compute on a single task, and then only later get to the point where it’s economical to use that capability routinely.

But whether that delay matters depends a lot on the application. If you’re doing some very valuable research task, you might be happy to spend a million dollars on an answer, provided you can check that it’s correct. If you’re answering ordinary customer support questions, that obviously doesn’t work. So there isn’t one threshold where a capability becomes practical; there are different thresholds for different uses.

And then there’s the question of how quickly the cost comes down. You can potentially improve the underlying model, make inference more efficient, or train on the successful outputs of an expensive process. So I wouldn’t assume that a capability which initially requires huge amounts of inference compute will remain expensive for very long. But I also wouldn’t assume that getting a good result with a huge search budget means you can immediately deploy it across the economy. Reliability, how you select the right answer, and the value of the task all matter.

r002.rationale: It says a capability may first be demonstrated with enormous compute and only later become economical to use routinely.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss pure pretraining scaling or immediate deployment across vast numbers of model instances.

r004.rationale: It suggests training on successful outputs from an expensive process and says such capabilities need not remain expensive for long, conveying that high-inference-compute capabilities may be distilled into cheaper-to-run models relatively quickly.
